pll1d22c4-d1e3501.summary: States that names proper to single persons (Father, Son, their Gift the Spirit) are said relatively to each other, while names of essential unity are said 'ad se,' substantially, of all together and each singly, and singularly, not plurally, in sum: God, good, powerful, great. Relative names are not said substantially.
claims: Essential names are said substantially and in the singular.
Relative names are not said substantially.

pll1d22c4-d1e3504.summary: Cites De Trinitate V: whatever God is said 'ad se' is said substantially; what is said 'ad aliquid' is said relatively. Such is the unity of substance that what is said of each 'ad se' is taken singularly in sum: Father, Son, and Spirit are each God, but not three Gods; each great, but not three greats; each omnipotent, but not three omnipotents. Since for God to be is to be great, we say one essence and one magnitude, not three.
claims: What is said 'ad se' of God is said substantially.
Essential predicates of each person are not plural in sum.
For God, being is being great.

pll1d22c4-d1e3524.summary: Continues Augustine: God is not great by a magnitude other than himself, as if participating it, or that magnitude would be greater than God. He is great by the magnitude he is, not by participation. The same holds of goodness, eternity, omnipotence, and all substantial names said properly, not metaphorically, if indeed anything can be said properly of God by human speech.
claims: God is great by the magnitude he is, not by participation.
The same holds for all substantial attributes.
It is uncertain whether anything can be said properly of God by humans.

pll1d22c4-d1e3537.summary: Concludes: names signifying divine unity are said of God 'ad se,' without relation, of all persons together and each singly, and singularly in sum; names proper to single persons are said relatively, not substantially, since, as Augustine says, what is said properly of each person is said in relation to another or to creatures.
claims: Essential names are said without relation and in the singular.
Personal names are said relatively, to another person or to creatures.

pl-l1d22c4.summary: Explains relative and absolute names. Names proper to single persons (Father, Son, Gift) are said relatively; names signifying the unity of essence are said 'ad se' and substantially, of all together and each singly, and in the singular in sum: Deus, bonus, potens, magnus. With Augustine, whatever is said 'ad se' is said substantially, and what is said relatively is not; Father, Son, and Spirit are each God, great, and omnipotent, yet not three Gods, greats, or omnipotents. God is great not by participating a magnitude other than himself, but is his own magnitude, and likewise for goodness, eternity, and all substantial names said properly, if anything can be said properly of God.
claims: Personal names are said relatively; essential names are said 'ad se' and substantially.
Essential names are said of each person and of all, but in the singular, not plural.
Father, Son, and Spirit are each God, great, and omnipotent, yet not three Gods, greats, or omnipotents.
God is great not by participation but by being his own magnitude.
Relative names are not said substantially.
